screens.title: Inheritance and Polymorphism
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we explore two foundational object-oriented tools that make game code reusable and flexible: inheritance and polymorphism. You will see how a common base class captures shared data and behavior, while specialized derived classes extend or replace that behavior when needed. This matters in game development because it keeps your code smaller, easier to maintain, and ready to accept new types — for example, adding a new enemy or weapon without rewriting core systems. We'll work through C# patterns such as calling the base constructor, using protected setters, and enabling method overriding with virtual and override. You'll also see a practical demonstration where a list of base-class references calls the same method on objects of different actual types and each object runs its own implementation. Finally, we briefly cover abstract classes and interfaces to show when to force derived classes to implement required behavior. After this lesson you'll be able to design simple hierarchies, avoid common inheritance mistakes, and use polymorphism to write extensible game systems.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Inheritance & Polymorphism
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Inheritance and Polymorphism

Create base classes to share data and methods, derive specialized types, and let runtime dispatch choose the right implementation. These patterns keep game logic extensible and maintainable.

Concept map
Base → Derived → Override
Base: Character — shared fields & methods
Derived: Player / Enemy — extend or override
Polymorphism: Call methods on base references
Explore Key Topics
Inheritance
Share fields and methods by deriving from a base class to avoid duplicate code.
Polymorphism
Let different objects handle the same method call in their own way at runtime.
Design Choices
Pick inheritance, composition, or interfaces based on reuse and flexibility needs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these lessons you will be able to apply inheritance and polymorphism to design cleaner game code. First, you'll implement inheritance to create derived classes from a common base class and use base constructors to initialize shared state. Second, you'll reason about the 'is-a' relationship so you choose inheritance only when it represents a real subtype. Third, you'll use the virtual and override keywords to enable runtime method selection, letting different objects respond appropriately to the same call. Fourth, you'll design simple class hierarchies for characters, enemies, and items so systems like combat can operate on a uniform base type. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or example to make it practical: implementing a Character base class, avoiding overuse of inheritance, using virtual for methods you expect to override, and organizing weapons, players, and enemies so they work with shared systems. These skills reduce duplication, make adding new entity types easier, and prevent brittle code in larger projects.

screens.title: What is Inheritance?
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance is a structural mechanism that lets a class reuse code from another class by expressing a clear subtype relationship. The base class holds shared fields and behavior — for example Name, Health, and AttackPower — while derived classes inherit those members and can add or override functionality. Saying 'Player is a Character' or 'Enemy is a Character' expresses the is-a relationship: a derived class should be usable anywhere the base class is expected. This is more than naming; it affects how you design systems. If your inventory system expects an Item, any derived item should behave as an Item. A concrete example is a Character base class with a virtual TakeDamage method; Player and Enemy inherit that method and can override it to apply armor or special reactions. A common misconception is to use inheritance whenever two classes share some data. Instead, ask whether one type truly specializes the other. If the relationship is 'has-a' — a Player has an Inventory — composition is usually better. Takeaway: inheritance groups shared state and behavior, but only when a true subtype relation exists.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › What is Inheritance?
Definition

Inheritance lets a derived class acquire fields and methods from a base class, forming an 'is-a' relationship. Use this when one type is a specialized form of another.

Key points
  • Base class contains shared state and behavior to avoid duplication.
  • Derived classes add or change behavior while reusing the base members.
  • Design choice: prefer inheritance for real subtypes; use composition otherwise.
Key Takeaway

Use inheritance to express specialization and centralize shared code; avoid it for incidental reuse.

Concrete example
Imagine a Character base class with Name, Health, and AttackPower. Both Player and Enemy inherit these fields so combat code can treat them the same.
Analogy
Think of a vehicle blueprint: Car and Motorcycle are both vehicles, so shared controls belong in Vehicle, while engine specifics go in each subtype.
Common mistake
Applying inheritance because two classes share a field instead of because one truly specializes the other. That leads to rigid deep hierarchies.

screens.title: C# Inheritance Syntax and base constructors
screens.narratorSegment: In C# you declare that a class derives from another using the colon operator. The derived class calls the base class constructor with base(...) so the base can initialize shared fields like Name and Health. A practical example from the chapter shows Character as the base class with a constructor that sets Name, Health, and AttackPower. Player then calls : base(name, health, attackPower) in its constructor to ensure the base logic runs and shared fields are initialized. This pattern prevents duplicated initialization code and guarantees the base invariants hold. Notice the use of protected set on properties — it allows derived classes to set values while keeping them read-only to other code. A common misconception is that derived class fields are independent; in reality, derived objects include the base object data so base constructors and initialization order matter. When designing constructors, always consider what the base needs to guarantee and expose a constructor that derived types can call safely. This makes object creation predictable and avoids subtle bugs at runtime. C# Inheritance Syntax and base constructors means use ': base(...)' to forward constructor parameters and protected setters to allow safe derived initialization.. In practical terms, how to declare derived classes and initialize shared state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › C# Inheritance Syntax
Code walkthrough (base & derived)
<!-- Note: angle brackets are escaped for safe display -->
<pre>
public class Character
{
    public string Name { get; protected set; }
    public int Health { get; protected set; }
    public int AttackPower { get; protected set; }

    public Character(string name, int health, int attackPower)
    {
        Name = name;
        Health = health;
        AttackPower = attackPower;
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name} (Health: {Health}, Attack: {AttackPower}) created.");
    }
}

public class Player : Character
{
    public Player(string name, int health, int attackPower)
        : base(name, health, attackPower)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name} is ready for adventure!");
    }
}
</pre>
Explanation
  • Use public ClassA : ClassB to inherit members from ClassB.
  • Derived constructors call base(...) to run base initialization logic first.
  • Protected setters let derived types mutate properties during construction while keeping them encapsulated.
Pro tip
Always consider what invariants the base constructor must establish, and expose only the parameters derived classes should supply.
Check your understanding
If a derived class forgets to call a required base constructor overload, the object may initialize incorrectly or fail to compile. Verify constructor signatures when refactoring.

screens.title: virtual and override keywords
screens.narratorSegment: The virtual and override keywords are the mechanism that makes polymorphic behavior possible in C#. When you mark a base class method as virtual, you signal that derived classes may provide a different implementation. The derived class uses override to replace that method. For example, Character. TakeDamage might be virtual, while Player overrides TakeDamage to apply armor and reduce incoming damage. The override can still call base. TakeDamage to reuse the base logic after applying its special handling. A common pitfall is to forget virtual in the base method; without it, override in derived classes is not allowed and runtime dispatch will not choose the derived implementation. Another pattern is to call protected helper methods from the base implementation and keep virtual only on those helpers if you want to limit what derived classes can change. Remember that virtual/override affect runtime dispatch: when code holds a reference typed as the base class, the actual object's override will execute. This separation between compile-time type and runtime type is what enables flexible game systems where new entity types can be added without modifying common loops or systems.

keyIdea.title: Behavior control
keyIdea.text: Mark base methods with virtual and replace them in derived classes with override to achieve runtime-specific behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › virtual & override
Pattern
Mark methods you expect to vary with virtual. Implement specialized behavior in derived classes using override. Optionally call base.Method() to reuse default behavior.
public virtual void TakeDamage(int damageAmount)
{
    Health -= damageAmount;
}

public override void TakeDamage(int damageAmount)
{
    int actual = Math.Max(0, damageAmount - 5);
    base.TakeDamage(actual);
}
Why it matters
  • Polymorphism depends on virtual/override for correct runtime dispatch.
  • Forgetting virtual prevents derived overrides from being used at runtime.
  • Use base calls when derived logic augments rather than replaces base behavior.
Common misconception
Some developers try to hide derived behavior using new instead of override; new hides the base method at compile time but does not enable polymorphism and often causes confusion.
Key Takeaway

Use virtual for methods you expect to customize and override in derived classes to implement type-specific behavior at runtime.

screens.title: Runtime dispatch with Lists of base types
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism shines when you write systems that operate on base-class references and accept new derived classes without change. The chapter shows a List containing Player and Enemy objects. When you iterate and call TakeDamage on each element, the runtime selects the correct implementation based on the object's actual type. This means your combat loop, AI manager, or rendering system can work with base types while individual types customize their behavior. A concrete example: create a Player with armor that reduces damage, and an Enemy that uses the base TakeDamage. Add both to a List, loop, and call TakeDamage(10). The Player's override runs and reduces damage first; the Enemy uses the base method. A frequent misunderstanding is expecting compile-time type to control which method runs; instead, C# uses the runtime type when the method is virtual. This allows you to add Boss or NPC classes later and have them participate in the same loops. Always ensure base methods you intend to be overridden are declared virtual so polymorphic dispatch happens correctly. Runtime dispatch with Lists of base types means a list of base-class references invokes the derived override at runtime, enabling flexible systems that accept new types.. In practical terms, how polymorphism lets systems treat different types uniformly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Polymorphism example
keyIdea.text: A List of base-class references invokes the derived override at runtime, enabling flexible systems that accept new types.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Polymorphism in Practice
Code sample: polymorphic loop
Player hero = new Player("Arthur", 100, 15);
Enemy goblin = new Enemy("Goblin Grunt", 40, 8, "Goblin");
Enemy orc = new Enemy("Orc Warrior", 150, 25, "Orc");

List<Character> combatants = new List<Character>();
combatants.Add(hero);
combatants.Add(goblin);
combatants.Add(orc);

foreach (Character c in combatants)
{
    c.TakeDamage(10);
}
When TakeDamage is called, the runtime inspects the actual object type and invokes Player's overridden method for the hero and Character's method for others, producing type-appropriate behavior without changing the loop.
Why this helps
  • Systems operate on the base type and remain unchanged as you add new derived types.
  • Encourages decoupling: combat loops needn't know subtype details.
  • Makes refactoring and extension safer and faster.
Misconception
Polymorphism is not compile-time overloading. The chosen method comes from runtime type when virtual methods are used.
Check

Try adding a Boss class with an override and see it participate with no loop changes.

screens.title: Abstract classes and interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Abstract classes and interfaces help you design systems that are flexible and clear about responsibilities. An abstract class can provide shared fields and concrete behavior but remain uninstantiable, forcing derived classes to supply specific implementations for abstract methods. This is useful when you have a common template with a required step that differs per subtype. An interface, by contrast, is a contract listing methods and properties a class must implement and allows unrelated types to share capabilities; for example, IDamageable can be implemented by characters, destructible scenery, or traps. Use abstract classes when you want some shared implementation and state; use interfaces when you want multiple unrelated capabilities on a single class. A common mistake is using abstract classes when multiple inheritance of behavior is necessary — interfaces provide that flexibility because a class can implement many interfaces. In Unity, interfaces are handy for decoupling systems like damage dealers from specific entity types. Takeaway: pick abstract classes for shared implementation, interfaces for cross-cutting capabilities. Abstract classes and interfaces means use abstract classes to provide shared implementation templates; use interfaces to express capabilities across unrelated types.. In practical terms, when to force implementations and when to express capabilities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Abstract Classes & Interfaces
Abstract class
Provides shared fields and some method bodies, but can include abstract methods that derived types must implement. Cannot be instantiated directly.
When to use
When multiple types share implementation details and must also provide type-specific behavior for certain methods.
Interface
Defines a contract of methods and properties. A class can implement multiple interfaces, expressing many capabilities.
When to use
When unrelated types need to present the same capability, like IDamageable for anything that can take damage.
Example
Use an abstract BaseEnemy to provide health and a default Attack, and implement IMoveable and IDamageable on components that require those behaviors. This keeps responsibilities clear and lets components combine capabilities.
Key Takeaway

Choose abstract classes for shared behavior and interfaces for capabilities you want to apply across unrelated types or multiple inheritance scenarios.

screens.title: Inheritance vs Composition
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent design decision is whether to use inheritance or composition. Inheritance models an is-a relationship: a Player is a Character, so inheritance makes sense. Composition models has-a: a Player has an Inventory or has a Weapon. Composition tends to produce more flexible designs because you can swap components at runtime and avoid deep, brittle class hierarchies. Consider a weapon system: instead of deriving many weapon types from Player, use a Weapon component the Player holds. However, inheritance is useful when many derived types share a significant amount of implementation and represent clear subtypes. The error is using inheritance because two classes share a single field. That leads to 'inheritance hell' with long hierarchies that are hard to change. A practical rule: prefer composition when behavior is orthogonal or changeable, prefer inheritance when a true specialization relationship exists and code reuse is substantial. Example: Character base class for shared combat fields, Weapon as a composed component that can be swapped on an entity. This hybrid approach often gives the best trade-offs. Inheritance vs Composition means use composition for flexible, swappable behavior; use inheritance when types truly specialize a base with substantial shared implementation.. In practical terms, when to extend a class and when to include behavior via composition. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Inheritance vs Composition
Inheritance (is-a)
  • Good when derived types are specialized forms of the base.
  • Centralizes shared implementation and fields.
  • Can become rigid if overused.
Composition (has-a)
  • Good for swapping behavior at runtime (e.g., weapons, abilities).
  • Promotes loose coupling and easier testing.
  • Often combines well with small inheritance where needed.
Scenario
You need a character that can equip different weapons and also several specialized enemy types. Use a Character base class for shared combat state, but treat Weapon as a composable component so you can add new weapons without changing the inheritance tree.
Takeaway
Prefer composition unless there is a strong subtype relationship and significant shared implementation to justify inheritance.

screens.title: Weapon hierarchy lab — code template

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Weapon Hierarchy Lab
Starter code template
public class Weapon
{
    public string Name { get; protected set; }
    public int Damage { get; protected set; }

    public Weapon(string name, int damage)
    {
        Name = name;
        Damage = damage;
    }

    public virtual int Attack()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name} performs a generic attack for {Damage} damage.");
        return Damage;
    }
}

public class Sword : Weapon
{
    public Sword() : base("Iron Sword", 10) { }

    public override int Attack()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Swings the {Name} for {Damage} damage!");
        return Damage;
    }
}

public class Bow : Weapon
{
    public Bow() : base("Wooden Bow", 7) { }

    public override int Attack()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Fires an arrow from the {Name} for {Damage} damage!");
        return Damage;
    }
}
Run scenario
Create objects, add them to a List<Weapon>, iterate and call Attack. Confirm the output shows the correct swing or fire messages from each override.
Expected behavior
Each Attack call prints the type-appropriate message and returns the damage value defined in the derived constructor.
Try expanding the lab: add a MagicStaff that overrides Attack to apply a status effect, or switch to Unity and place weapons as components that the Player composes at runtime.

screens.title: Inheritance in Unity scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Unity scripts typically inherit from MonoBehaviour, which acts as a common base for Unity components. The chapter reminds us that Unity's lifecycle methods like Start and Update are not virtual in the usual way, but you can create your own custom base classes that inherit from MonoBehaviour and declare virtual methods for your game logic. For example, a BaseEnemy MonoBehaviour could define health, speed, and a virtual Attack method. MeleeEnemy and RangedEnemy derive from BaseEnemy and override Attack to implement slashes or shots. This approach centralizes shared data and gives you control over what behaviors can be customized. When designing MonoBehaviour hierarchies, be cautious: deep inheritance with engine components can complicate inspector fields and serialization. A safer pattern is to keep MonoBehaviour subclasses shallow and move shared logic into plain C# base classes when possible. This preserves Unity editor friendliness while still benefiting from inheritance and polymorphism for game logic. Pattern

screens.title: Pitfalls and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Developers commonly fall into two traps with inheritance. The first is overusing inheritance to copy-shared fields across many classes rather than modeling true subtypes. This often produces deep hierarchies that are hard to change and understand, an outcome sometimes called 'inheritance hell.' The second trap is forgetting to mark base methods virtual or failing to use override in derived classes. If a base method is not virtual, derived classes cannot override it to provide polymorphic behavior; similarly, using new hides a method at compile time without enabling polymorphism and leads to confusing behavior. Best practices include: prefer composition for swappable behavior, mark only methods you intend to override as virtual, use protected setters and base calls responsibly, and keep MonoBehaviour inheritance shallow in Unity projects. When in doubt, sketch a small class diagram and ask whether an object of the derived type can truly substitute for the base in all expected contexts. Pitfalls and best practices means avoid deep hierarchies, ensure virtual is used where needed, prefer composition for swappable behavior, and keep engine inheritance shallow.. In practical terms, avoid inheritance hell and missing virtual/override keywords. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Overuse of inheritance
Don't inherit just to reuse a field. If the relation is not a true subtype, use composition instead.

Review a small design and ask: can an instance of the derived type be used wherever the base is expected? If yes, inheritance may be appropriate. If behavior must change or swap at runtime, consider composition instead.

Question
If Vehicle.StartEngine is virtual and Car wants to provide its own start logic, which keyword does Car use?
Options
  • a) new
  • b) base

Answer explained
The correct answer is override. virtual belongs in the base; override replaces the virtual method in the derived class and enables polymorphic behavior at runtime. new only hides the method at compile time and does not participate in polymorphism.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. Inheritance allows a derived class to acquire fields and methods from a base class, forming an is-a relationship and centralizing shared behavior. The virtual and override keywords enable polymorphism by allowing derived classes to replace base behavior. At runtime, method calls on base-typed references dispatch to the actual object's override, which is how systems remain flexible. Abstract classes and interfaces are tools for forcing implementation or expressing capabilities across unrelated types. Finally, design decisions matter: prefer composition for swappable behavior and keep MonoBehaviour hierarchies shallow in Unity projects to avoid editor and serialization surprises. These are not merely language features; they are design levers that affect maintainability and extensibility. Keep practicing with small labs like the Weapon hierarchy to make these ideas concrete.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we explore two foundational object-oriented tools that make game code reusable and flexible: inheritance and polymorphism. You will see how a common base class captures shared data and behavior, while specialized derived classes extend or replace that behavior when needed. This matters in game development because it keeps your code smaller, easier to maintain, and ready to accept new types — for example, adding a new enemy or weapon without rewriting core systems. We'll work through C# patterns such as calling the base constructor, using protected setters, and enabling method overriding with virtual and override. You'll also see a practical demonstration where a list of base-class references calls the same method on objects of different actual types and each object runs its own implementation. Finally, we briefly cover abstract classes and interfaces to show when to force derived classes to implement required behavior. After this lesson you'll be able to design simple hierarchies, avoid common inheritance mistakes, and use polymorphism to write extensible game systems.

By the end of these lessons you will be able to apply inheritance and polymorphism to design cleaner game code. First, you'll implement inheritance to create derived classes from a common base class and use base constructors to initialize shared state. Second, you'll reason about the 'is-a' relationship so you choose inheritance only when it represents a real subtype. Third, you'll use the virtual and override keywords to enable runtime method selection, letting different objects respond appropriately to the same call. Fourth, you'll design simple class hierarchies for characters, enemies, and items so systems like combat can operate on a uniform base type. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or example to make it practical: implementing a Character base class, avoiding overuse of inheritance, using virtual for methods you expect to override, and organizing weapons, players, and enemies so they work with shared systems. These skills reduce duplication, make adding new entity types easier, and prevent brittle code in larger projects.

These objectives focus on practical design and application. You will learn to call base constructors so inherited state initializes correctly, and to use protected accessors to let derived classes modify important fields without exposing them publicly. You will practice designing weapon and enemy hierarchies that demonstrate polymorphism by iterating over a list of base references. You'll also be introduced to abstract classes and interfaces to know when to force derived classes to implement required behavior or to allow multiple capabilities. Each objective ties to a hands-on activity: building a Weapon base class with Sword and Bow derived types, and looping through a list to call Attack on each weapon. This practice helps you understand both the mechanics of syntax and the design judgment that prevents overusing inheritance. Finally, you will review common mistakes and learn simple rules—prefer composition when the relationship is 'has-a', reserve inheritance for true subtyping, and ensure virtual is used where overrides are intended.

Inheritance is a structural mechanism that lets a class reuse code from another class by expressing a clear subtype relationship. The base class holds shared fields and behavior — for example Name, Health, and AttackPower — while derived classes inherit those members and can add or override functionality. Saying 'Player is a Character' or 'Enemy is a Character' expresses the is-a relationship: a derived class should be usable anywhere the base class is expected. This is more than naming; it affects how you design systems. If your inventory system expects an Item, any derived item should behave as an Item. A concrete example is a Character base class with a virtual TakeDamage method; Player and Enemy inherit that method and can override it to apply armor or special reactions. A common misconception is to use inheritance whenever two classes share some data. Instead, ask whether one type truly specializes the other. If the relationship is 'has-a' — a Player has an Inventory — composition is usually better. Takeaway: inheritance groups shared state and behavior, but only when a true subtype relation exists.

In C# you declare that a class derives from another using the colon operator. The derived class calls the base class constructor with base(...) so the base can initialize shared fields like Name and Health. A practical example from the chapter shows Character as the base class with a constructor that sets Name, Health, and AttackPower. Player then calls : base(name, health, attackPower) in its constructor to ensure the base logic runs and shared fields are initialized. This pattern prevents duplicated initialization code and guarantees the base invariants hold. Notice the use of protected set on properties — it allows derived classes to set values while keeping them read-only to other code. A common misconception is that derived class fields are independent; in reality, derived objects include the base object data so base constructors and initialization order matter. When designing constructors, always consider what the base needs to guarantee and expose a constructor that derived types can call safely. This makes object creation predictable and avoids subtle bugs at runtime. C# Inheritance Syntax and base constructors means use ': base(...)' to forward constructor parameters and protected setters to allow safe derived initialization.. In practical terms, how to declare derived classes and initialize shared state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The virtual and override keywords are the mechanism that makes polymorphic behavior possible in C#. When you mark a base class method as virtual, you signal that derived classes may provide a different implementation. The derived class uses override to replace that method. For example, Character. TakeDamage might be virtual, while Player overrides TakeDamage to apply armor and reduce incoming damage. The override can still call base. TakeDamage to reuse the base logic after applying its special handling. A common pitfall is to forget virtual in the base method; without it, override in derived classes is not allowed and runtime dispatch will not choose the derived implementation. Another pattern is to call protected helper methods from the base implementation and keep virtual only on those helpers if you want to limit what derived classes can change. Remember that virtual/override affect runtime dispatch: when code holds a reference typed as the base class, the actual object's override will execute. This separation between compile-time type and runtime type is what enables flexible game systems where new entity types can be added without modifying common loops or systems.

Polymorphism shines when you write systems that operate on base-class references and accept new derived classes without change. The chapter shows a List containing Player and Enemy objects. When you iterate and call TakeDamage on each element, the runtime selects the correct implementation based on the object's actual type. This means your combat loop, AI manager, or rendering system can work with base types while individual types customize their behavior. A concrete example: create a Player with armor that reduces damage, and an Enemy that uses the base TakeDamage. Add both to a List, loop, and call TakeDamage(10). The Player's override runs and reduces damage first; the Enemy uses the base method. A frequent misunderstanding is expecting compile-time type to control which method runs; instead, C# uses the runtime type when the method is virtual. This allows you to add Boss or NPC classes later and have them participate in the same loops. Always ensure base methods you intend to be overridden are declared virtual so polymorphic dispatch happens correctly. Runtime dispatch with Lists of base types means a list of base-class references invokes the derived override at runtime, enabling flexible systems that accept new types.. In practical terms, how polymorphism lets systems treat different types uniformly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Abstract classes and interfaces help you design systems that are flexible and clear about responsibilities. An abstract class can provide shared fields and concrete behavior but remain uninstantiable, forcing derived classes to supply specific implementations for abstract methods. This is useful when you have a common template with a required step that differs per subtype. An interface, by contrast, is a contract listing methods and properties a class must implement and allows unrelated types to share capabilities; for example, IDamageable can be implemented by characters, destructible scenery, or traps. Use abstract classes when you want some shared implementation and state; use interfaces when you want multiple unrelated capabilities on a single class. A common mistake is using abstract classes when multiple inheritance of behavior is necessary — interfaces provide that flexibility because a class can implement many interfaces. In Unity, interfaces are handy for decoupling systems like damage dealers from specific entity types. Takeaway: pick abstract classes for shared implementation, interfaces for cross-cutting capabilities. Abstract classes and interfaces means use abstract classes to provide shared implementation templates; use interfaces to express capabilities across unrelated types.. In practical terms, when to force implementations and when to express capabilities. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A frequent design decision is whether to use inheritance or composition. Inheritance models an is-a relationship: a Player is a Character, so inheritance makes sense. Composition models has-a: a Player has an Inventory or has a Weapon. Composition tends to produce more flexible designs because you can swap components at runtime and avoid deep, brittle class hierarchies. Consider a weapon system: instead of deriving many weapon types from Player, use a Weapon component the Player holds. However, inheritance is useful when many derived types share a significant amount of implementation and represent clear subtypes. The error is using inheritance because two classes share a single field. That leads to 'inheritance hell' with long hierarchies that are hard to change. A practical rule: prefer composition when behavior is orthogonal or changeable, prefer inheritance when a true specialization relationship exists and code reuse is substantial. Example: Character base class for shared combat fields, Weapon as a composed component that can be swapped on an entity. This hybrid approach often gives the best trade-offs. Developers commonly fall into two traps with inheritance. The first is overusing inheritance to copy-shared fields across many classes rather than modeling true subtypes. This often produces deep hierarchies that are hard to change and understand, an outcome sometimes called 'inheritance hell.' The second trap is forgetting to mark base methods virtual or failing to use override in derived classes. If a base method is not virtual, derived classes cannot override it to provide polymorphic behavior; similarly, using new hides a method at compile time without enabling polymorphism and leads to confusing behavior. Best practices include: prefer composition for swappable behavior, mark only methods you intend to override as virtual, use protected setters and base calls responsibly, and keep MonoBehaviour inheritance shallow in Unity projects. Let's summarize the essential concepts to carry forward. Inheritance allows a derived class to acquire fields and methods from a base class, forming an is-a relationship and centralizing shared behavior. The virtual and override keywords enable polymorphism by allowing derived classes to replace base behavior. At runtime, method calls on base-typed references dispatch to the actual object's override, which is how systems remain flexible. Abstract classes and interfaces are tools for forcing implementation or expressing capabilities across unrelated types. Finally, design decisions matter: prefer composition for swappable behavior and keep MonoBehaviour hierarchies shallow in Unity projects to avoid editor and serialization surprises. These are not merely language features; they are design levers that affect maintainability and extensibility. Keep practicing with small labs like the Weapon hierarchy to make these ideas concrete.

Finish with three concise reminders. First, inheritance groups shared fields and methods in a base class so derived types can reuse them; use it only for true subtypes. Second, virtual in the base and override in derived classes enable polymorphism so systems can call methods on base types and let the actual object choose the right behavior. Third, interfaces and abstract classes are design tools: abstract classes provide a shared template and implementation, while interfaces express capabilities across unrelated types. Keep these three ideas in mind as you design game entities: apply the right tool for the right problem, test polymorphism with small lists, and avoid deep, rigid hierarchies by favoring composition when behavior should be swappable.
